extracted.intended_audience: Cambridge IGCSE English examiners (and teachers/candidates using the mark scheme)
extracted.subtask_description: Marking guidance and assessment criteria for Cambridge IGCSE First Language English Paper 2 (Directed Writing and Composition), including generic marking principles, assessment objectives, task-specific instructions and level descriptors for award of marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: GENERIC MARKING PRINCIPLE 1
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks must be awarded in line with: the specific content of the mark scheme or the generic level descriptors for the question; the specific skills defined in the mark scheme or in the generic level descriptors for the question; the standard of response required by a candidate as exemplified by the standardisation scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: GENERIC MARKING PRINCIPLE 2
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks awarded are always whole marks (not half marks, or other fractions).

rubrics_metrics.name: GENERIC MARKING PRINCIPLE 3 (award positively)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks must be awarded positively: marks are awarded for correct/valid answers as defined in the mark scheme; credit is given for valid answers which go beyond the scope of the syllabus and mark scheme (refer to Team Leader as appropriate); marks are awarded when candidates clearly demonstrate what they know and can do; marks are not deducted for errors; marks are not deducted for omissions; answers should only be judged on the quality of spelling, punctuation and grammar when these features are specifically assessed by the question as indicated by the mark scheme; the meaning, however, should be unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: GENERIC MARKING PRINCIPLE 4 (consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules must be applied consistently, e.g. in situations where candidates have not followed instructions or in the application of generic level descriptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: GENERIC MARKING PRINCIPLE 5 (use full range)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks should be awarded using the full range of marks defined in the mark scheme for the question (however; the use of the full mark range may be limited according to the quality of the candidate responses seen).

rubrics_metrics.name: GENERIC MARKING PRINCIPLE 6 (marks only on defined requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks awarded are based solely on the requirements as defined in the mark scheme. Marks should not be awarded with grade thresholds or grade descriptors in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative/Unexpected answers guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: All examiners are instructed that alternative correct answers and unexpected approaches in candidates’ scripts must be given marks that fairly reflect the relevant knowledge and skills demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonetheless, the content must be clearly related to and derived from the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: W1 (Writing assessment objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: W1 articulate experience and express what is thought, felt and imagined

rubrics_metrics.name: W2 (Writing assessment objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: W2 organise and structure ideas and opinions for deliberate effect

rubrics_metrics.name: W3 (Writing assessment objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: W3 use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures appropriate to context

rubrics_metrics.name: W4 (Writing assessment objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: W4 use register appropriate to context

rubrics_metrics.name: W5 (Writing assessment objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: W5 make accurate use of spelling, punctuation and grammar.

rubrics_metrics.name: R1 (Reading assessment objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: R1 demonstrate understanding of explicit meanings

rubrics_metrics.name: R2 (Reading assessment objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: R2 demonstrate understanding of implicit meanings and attitudes

rubrics_metrics.name: R3 (Reading assessment objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: R3 analyse, evaluate and develop facts, ideas and opinions, using appropriate support from the text

rubrics_metrics.name: R5 (Reading assessment objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: R5 select and use information for specific purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed Writing Task requirements (Question 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a speech (beginning 'Thank you for coming to listen to me today ...') to be given in a school assembly on whether or not students should participate in decisions made about the school. Base your speech on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words, address both bullet points, and write about 250 to 350 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In your speech you should: evaluate the views given in both texts about student participation; give your own views, based on what you have read, about whether a school council would benefit students and teachers. Up to 15 marks for content and up to 25 marks for quality of writing (total 40).

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed Writing: Acceptable content ideas (Text A guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested ideas candidates might use from Text A include: 'once fashionable' – student representation may just be a passing fad; School councils take up too much time and energy from students and teachers; 'lip service' – if student representation is fake, it has no substance; Teachers are accountable to parents and should put education first; Experienced teachers should make decisions, not children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are example content points; responses must be based on the texts but in candidates' own words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed Writing: Acceptable content ideas (Text B guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested ideas candidates might use from Text B include: An 'enlightened' approach is needed to make school councils work; Student participation is very popular and well regarded; Student participation works when children are involved in 'real' issues; Students can take responsibility for difficult problems, e.g. behaviour; Participation can make a difference to students' attitudes to school; Attendance and results are improved by participation; Students can learn important skills, e.g. negotiation, communication, decision-making; Students can have a fresh eye on issues; Decisions made may have a major impact on them so they are motivated to participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are suggested content ideas to help candidates evaluate and synthesise the texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed Writing: Possible evaluation and synthesis guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible evaluation points: Text A may show that school councils are pointless if students' decisions are not valued; Mr Aziz suggests students have little experience to bring to decisions about school; the main function of a school is to educate – this has implications for student participation. Text B: student representation on its own is not enough – needs planning; some quite ambitious claims are made about its benefits – are these realistic? Not much is said about how much time and commitment it takes – just that it should be spelt out. Possible synthesis: Text A and Text B illustrate different approaches (teacher authority vs teacher as facilitator); both extremes possible and truth may lie between; the 'it all depends' approach may show synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This section is guidance to examiners and candidates on lines of response that demonstrate evaluation and synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Writing (Table A) Level 6 (22–25 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly effective style capable of conveying subtle meaning. Carefully structured for benefit of the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wide range of sophisticated vocabulary, precisely used (W3); Highly effective register for audience and purpose (W4); Spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate (W5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Writing (Table A) Level 5 (18–21 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective style. Secure overall structure, organised to help the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wide range of vocabulary, used with some precision (W3); Effective register for audience and purpose (W4); Spelling, punctuation and grammar mostly accurate, with occasional minor errors (W5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Writing (Table A) Level 4 (14–17 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes effective style. Ideas generally well sequenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Range of vocabulary is adequate and sometimes effective (W3); Sometimes effective register for audience and purpose (W4); Spelling, punctuation and grammar generally accurate though with some errors (W5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Writing (Table A) Level 3 (10–13 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsistent style, expression sometimes awkward but meaning clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relies on the sequence of the original text (W2); Vocabulary is simple, limited in range or reliant on the original text (W3); Some awareness of an appropriate register for audience and purpose (W4); Frequent errors of spelling, punctuation and grammar, sometimes serious (W5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Writing (Table A) Level 2 (6–9 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited style. Response is not well sequenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited vocabulary or words/phrases copied from the original text (W3); Limited awareness of appropriate register for audience and purpose (W4); Persistent errors of spelling, punctuation and grammar (W5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Writing (Table A) Level 1 (1–5 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression unclear. Poor sequencing of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very limited vocabulary or copying from the original text (W3); Very limited awareness of appropriate register for audience and purpose (W4); Persistent errors in spelling, punctuation and grammar impede communication (W5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Writing (Table A) Level 0 (0 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: No creditable content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Reading (Table B) Level 6 (13–15 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successfully evaluates ideas and opinions, both explicit and implicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assimilates ideas from the text to give a developed, sophisticated response (R3, R5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Reading (Table B) Level 5 (10–12 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some successful evaluation of ideas and opinions, both explicit and implicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thorough response, supported by a detailed selection of relevant ideas from the text (R3, R5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Reading (Table B) Level 4 (7–9 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begins to evaluate mainly explicit ideas and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appropriate response that includes relevant ideas from the text (R3, R5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Reading (Table B) Level 3 (5–6 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selects and comments on explicit ideas and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Makes a general response including a few relevant ideas from the text (R3, R5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Reading (Table B) Level 2 (3–4 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifies explicit ideas and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Makes a limited response with little evidence from the text (R3, R5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Reading (Table B) Level 1 (1–2 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Very limited response with minimal relation to the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section A — Reading (Table B) Level 0 (0 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: No creditable content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section B — Composition task format and marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition questions (2–5) each worth 40 marks. Use Table A to give a mark out of 16 for content and structure, and Table B to give a mark out of 24 for style and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition options include descriptive prompts (e.g. eating together, busy station) and narrative prompts (stories including a given line or involving a new character).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table A — Content and structure Level 6 (14–16 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: General: Content is complex, engaging and effective. Structure is secure, well balanced and carefully managed for deliberate effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific – descriptive: Many well-defined and developed ideas and images create a convincing overall picture with varieties of focus. Specific – narrative: The plot is well-defined and strongly developed with features of fiction writing such as description, characterisation and effective climax, and convincing details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table A — Content and structure Level 5 (11–13 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: General: Content is developed, engaging and effective. Structure is well managed, with some choices made for deliberate effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific – descriptive: Frequent, well-chosen images and details give a mostly convincing picture. Specific – narrative: The plot is defined and developed with features of fiction writing such as description, characterisation, climax and details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table A — Content and structure Level 4 (8–10 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: General: Content is relevant with some development. Structure is competently managed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific – descriptive: A selection of relevant ideas, images and details, even where there is a tendency to write in a narrative style. Specific – narrative: The plot is relevant and cohesive, with some features such as characterisation and setting of scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table A — Content and structure Level 3 (5–7 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: General: Content is straightforward and briefly developed. Structure is mostly organised but may not always be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific – descriptive: The task is addressed with a series of relevant but straightforward details, which may be more typical of a narrative. Specific – narrative: The plot is straightforward, with limited use of the features of narrative writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table A — Content and structure Level 2 (3–4 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: General: Content is simple, and ideas and events may be limited. Structure is partially organised but limited in its effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific – descriptive: The recording of some relevant events with limited detail. Specific – narrative: The plot is a simple narrative that may consist of events that are only partially linked and/or which are presented with partial clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table A — Content and structure Level 1 (1–2 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: General: Content is occasionally relevant or clear. Structure is limited and ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific – descriptive: The description is unclear and lacks detail. Specific – narrative: The plot and/or narrative lacks coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table A — Content and structure Level 0 (0 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: No creditable content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table B — Style and accuracy Level 6 (21–24 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Precise, well-chosen vocabulary and varied sentence structures, chosen for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent well-chosen register suitable for the context (W4); Spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate (W5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table B — Style and accuracy Level 5 (17–20 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mostly precise vocabulary and a range of sentence structures mostly used for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mostly consistent appropriate register suitable for the context (W4); Spelling, punctuation and grammar mostly accurate, with occasional minor errors (W5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table B — Style and accuracy Level 4 (13–16 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some precise vocabulary and a range of sentence structures sometimes used for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some appropriate register for the context (W4); Spelling, punctuation and grammar generally accurate, but with some errors (W5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table B — Style and accuracy Level 3 (9–12 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple vocabulary and a range of straightforward sentence structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple register with a general awareness of the context (W4); Frequent errors of spelling, punctuation and grammar, occasionally serious (W5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table B — Style and accuracy Level 2 (5–8 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited and/or imprecise vocabulary and sentence structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited and/or imprecise register for the context (W4); Persistent errors of spelling, punctuation and grammar (W5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table B — Style and accuracy Level 1 (1–4 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequently imprecise vocabulary and sentence structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Register demonstrates little or no sense of the context (W4); Persistent errors of spelling, punctuation and grammar impair communication (W5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Table B — Style and accuracy Level 0 (0 marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: No creditable content.
